issues.legal_issue: A civil court’s possession finding in a criminal possession reference is final and cannot be challenged by appeal, review, or revision.
material_facts: A magistrate referred the disputed possession issue to a civil court after being unable to determine which side was in possession.
The civil court found that one side was in possession, and the finding was challenged.
issues.conclusion: The civil court’s finding on possession was final and could not be challenged by appeal, review, or revision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 146(1D) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 expressly bars an appeal, review, or revision against a civil court’s finding on a reference under that section. The bar applies even though the referring court remains a civil court. State of U.P. v. Ramachandra Aggarwal was followed.

predicates.criminal_possession_reference_proceeding: A magistrate referred a disputed possession issue to a civil court in a criminal proceeding concerning possession.
predicates.civil_court_made_possession_finding: The civil court made a finding about which side was in possession.

issues.definition: When a magistrate refers a possession dispute to a civil court and that court makes a possession finding, the finding cannot be challenged by appeal, review, or revision.

issues.legal_issue: A magistrate’s order that conforms to a civil court’s possession finding cannot be challenged in criminal revision.
material_facts: After receiving the civil court’s finding, the magistrate made an order in conformity with it.
The opposing side sought revision of the magistrate’s order, challenging the basis of the order in the civil court’s finding.
issues.conclusion: The conforming order could not be challenged under Sections 435 and 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898; the High Court could intervene if the magistrate’s order did not conform to the civil court’s finding.
issues.legal_principle: Section 146(1B) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 requires the magistrate to dispose of the proceeding in conformity with the civil court’s decision. Sections 435 and 439 do not permit revision of an order that complies with that requirement as a means of challenging the civil court’s finding; the High Court may examine whether the magistrate’s order conforms to that finding.

predicates.criminal_possession_reference_proceeding: A magistrate referred a disputed possession issue to a civil court in a criminal proceeding concerning possession.
predicates.magistrate_order_conforms_to_civil_findi: After receiving the civil court’s finding, the magistrate made an order consistent with that finding.

issues.definition: In a criminal possession reference, a magistrate’s order consistent with the civil court’s finding is not open to criminal revision.

issues.legal_issue: Constitutional superintendence cannot be used as appellate review to correct factual errors when the subordinate tribunal has acted within its authority.
material_facts: The civil court considered the parties’ affidavits and gave them no weight because the deponents were interested persons.
The magistrate’s order conformed to the civil court’s possession finding.
The High Court set aside the orders on the ground that the civil court had failed to consider the affidavits, and that ground treated the civil court’s factual assessment as open to re-examination.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s superintendence power was not curtailed by the procedural bar, but it could not be used to correct a factual error or act as an appellate court; the circumstances did not justify intervention.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 of the Constitution remains available notwithstanding restrictions in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, but its supervisory scope is limited to keeping subordinate courts and tribunals within the bounds of their authority. It does not permit correction of factual errors or conversion of the High Court into a court of appeal. Waryam Singh v. Amar Nath, Nagendra Nath Bora v. Commissioner of Hills Division and Appeals, Assam, and Babhutmal Raichand Oswal v. Laxmibai R. Tarts were reiterated.

predicates.supervisory_review_proceeding: A party invoked the High Court’s supervisory power to challenge an order made in a subordinate proceeding.
predicates.subordinate_court_within_authority: The subordinate court acted within the limits of its authority.
predicates.challenge_seeks_correction_of_factual_er: The challenge asks the High Court to re-examine or correct the subordinate court’s factual assessment.

issues.definition: When supervisory review is invoked against a subordinate court acting within its authority and the challenge concerns factual assessment, the High Court should not intervene as though it were an appellate court.
